nameStory: Smooth sawgrass gets its name from the saw-like edges found on many of its sedge relatives, though this species is notably 'smooth' with leaves that won't cut your fingers. The 'sawgrass' part comes from other Cladium species whose razor-sharp leaf edges can slice skin like a saw blade. It's nature's way of saying 'look but don't grab!'
description: Smooth sawgrass is a tall, grass-like sedge that forms colonies in wetlands throughout New England. This perennial plant grows up to 3 feet tall with very narrow leaves and spreads underground through creeping stems called rhizomes. Despite being called a grass, it's actually a sedge - you can tell because its stems are triangular rather than round. In late summer, it produces clusters of small, chestnut-brown flower spikes that help distinguish it from true grasses.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems are triangular in cross-section (not round like grasses) and feel solid when you gently squeeze them - try the 'sedges have edges' test by rolling the stem between your fingers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow leaves, less than an eighth-inch wide, that feel smooth to the touch and won't cut your skin like other sawgrass species - run your finger along the edge gently to test

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small chestnut-brown to reddish-brown flower clusters arranged in branching sprays at the top of stems, appearing in late summer and feeling papery when dry

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense colonies from underground rhizomes, creating patches of similar-height plants that can dominate wet areas

idTips.label: Height
idTips.description: Grows 2-3 feet tall on average, standing upright and swaying gently in wetland breezes

habitat: Look for smooth sawgrass in the soggy edges of ponds, marshes, and slow streams throughout New England's lowlands. It thrives in both freshwater wetlands and coastal salt marshes, often growing with cattails, sedges, and rushes. You'll find it with its 'feet wet' - always in areas that stay moist or flooded for much of the year.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from underground rhizomes, creating fresh colonies. Plants begin their rapid upward growth as wetlands warm.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height and develop their characteristic narrow leaves. Late summer brings the distinctive chestnut-brown flower clusters.
seasonality.fall: Flower heads turn deep brown and release seeds. Leaves begin to yellow and die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only dead brown stems that may persist. Underground rhizomes remain alive, ready for spring growth.

funFact: Despite its innocent name, smooth sawgrass is like the 'nice sibling' in a family of botanical razors - most other sawgrass species have leaves so sharp they're used by indigenous peoples to cut and slice materials, earning them the nickname 'nature's knife drawer.'
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other tall sedges and rushes in wetlands, but remember 'sedges have edges' - squeeze the stem gently and feel for the triangular shape that grasses and rushes lack. The chestnut-brown flower clusters are also distinctive from the more cylindrical or rounded flower heads of most other wetland plants.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - this isn't actually a grass at all, but a sedge! The sedge family often gets mistaken for grasses, but they're quite different plants. While this species is 'smooth,' be careful around its relatives in Florida and other southern areas, where sawgrass can literally cut like a knife.
compareHints: Smooth sawgrass is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique among local sawgrasses. Compared to other tall sedges in wetlands, it's distinguished by its very narrow leaves and distinctive branched clusters of chestnut-brown flowers. Most similar sedges have wider leaves or different colored flower heads - bulrushes have rounded brown heads, while other sedges often have greenish or tan flowers.
